lines.text:
The Frozen World — Life in the Arctic

The Arctic is one of the coldest places on Earth. Temperatures can drop below minus forty degrees, and for months in winter, there is no sunlight at all. Yet this frozen world is home to extraordinary animals, dramatic landscapes, and communities that have lived here for thousands of years.

The landscape is shaped by ice and snow. A glacier — a slow-moving river of ice — carves through mountains over centuries. An iceberg — a huge block of ice that has broken off a glacier — floats in the dark water, with most of its mass hidden below the surface. An ice sheet covers Greenland, kilometres thick in places. Pack ice drifts on the ocean, breaking apart in summer and refreezing in winter. A snowfield stretches to the horizon, white and flat. Icicles hang from cliffs. Frost coats every surface. Snowflakes fall silently. Slush forms where snow begins to melt. A crevasse — a deep crack in a glacier — is one of the most dangerous features for travellers.

Beyond the ice, the tundra — a vast, treeless plain — supports low plants, mosses, and grasses during the brief summer. A fjord — a long, narrow inlet carved by a glacier — cuts deep into the coastline. Frozen lakes, mountains, valleys, peninsulas, islands, bays, and steep cliffs define the Arctic geography.

Arctic animals are built for the cold. A polar bear — the largest land predator on Earth — hunts seals on the pack ice. Its white fur provides camouflage against the snow. An Arctic fox changes colour: white in winter, brown in summer. A walrus rests on the ice, its long tusks used for climbing and fighting. Seals swim beneath the ice and breathe through holes they keep open. A narwhal — sometimes called the 'unicorn of the sea' — has a long, spiralling tusk. A beluga whale is pure white and communicates with clicks and whistles. A snowy owl hunts lemmings across the tundra. A puffin nests on cliffsides. Reindeer travel in herds across the tundra, searching for food beneath the snow. An Arctic hare has thick fur and powerful back legs for running across snow.

Survival clothing is essential. A parka — a thick, hooded jacket — is the most important piece. Snow boots keep feet dry and warm. A fur hat covers the ears. Mittens are warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat. A scarf protects the face from wind. Thermal underwear is worn as a base layer. Goggles protect the eyes from snow blindness. A face mask shields the skin. Snow pants and wool socks complete the outfit.

Travel in the Arctic requires special vehicles. A dog sled — pulled by a team of dogs — is the traditional method. A snowmobile is faster but needs fuel. An icebreaker — a ship designed to push through pack ice — opens sea routes. A kayak is used for fishing in calm fjords. Skis allow quick movement across snowfields.

The Arctic is changing. Glaciers are shrinking. Pack ice is thinner. Animals like the polar bear are losing their hunting grounds. Understanding the Arctic — its beauty, its dangers, and its fragility — has never been more important.

lines.text: 'Very' + adjective: 'very cold', 'very dangerous.' 'Very much' + verb: 'I very much appreciate it.' Never 'very much cold' — 'very much' doesn't modify adjectives. 'Much' alone modifies comparatives: 'much colder', 'much bigger.'

lines.text: Never double-mark comparatives: 'bigger' (not *more bigger), 'colder' (not *more colder). Use 'much' or 'far' to intensify: 'much bigger', 'far colder.' 'More' is only for longer adjectives: 'more dangerous', 'more difficult.'

lines.text: Present perfect uses 'have/has + past participle.' 'See – saw – seen.' 'I have seen' (not *I have saw). 'I saw it yesterday' (past simple — no 'have'). Common errors: 'I have went' → 'I have gone.' 'I have did' → 'I have done.'

lines.text: 'Arctic' comes from the Greek word for 'bear' (arktos — referring to the constellation). 'Antarctic' means 'opposite the bear'. The Arctic is in the north; the Antarctic is in the south. They have different wildlife — penguins live only in the Antarctic, polar bears only in the Arctic.

lines.text: 'Inuit' (meaning 'the people') is the correct name for the indigenous peoples of the Arctic. 'Eskimo' is considered outdated and offensive by many Inuit. The plural is 'Inuit' (not 'Inuits'). Their language family is Inuktitut.

lines.text: 'Sub-zero' = below 0°C. 'Below freezing' = same meaning. 'Wind chill' = how cold it feels with wind. 'Frostbite' = injury from extreme cold. 'Hypothermia' = dangerously low body temperature. These are useful B2 vocabulary items.
